blocks.en: 📖 Bible Characters — Unit 7: Gideon — When God Wins With Few
blocks.es_reference: 📖 Personajes de la Biblia — Unidad 7: Gedeón — Cuando Dios Vence con Pocos

blocks.en: Professor: Dr. Wayne Cook | Director: Dr. Ted Rogers
blocks.es_reference: Profesor: Dr. Wayne Cook | Director: Dr. Ted Rogers

blocks.en: "Not by might nor by power, but by My Spirit," says the LORD of hosts. — Zechariah 4:6 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: «No con ejército, ni con fuerza, sino con mi Espíritu», ha dicho Jehová de los ejércitos. — Zacarías 4:6 (RVG)

blocks.en: When Israel had once again done evil, God handed them over to the Midianites, who swept across the land like a swarm of locusts, stripping the fields and driving the people into caves and dens in the mountains. It was into that desperate hour that God reached down and called the unlikeliest of deliverers — a frightened farmer named Gideon. His story is one of the clearest lessons in all of Scripture about how God works: He deliberately strips away every advantage we lean on, until the only possible explanation for the victory is God Himself. When the battle is won with a handful of men and no swords, no one can say, "My own hand has saved me."
blocks.es_reference: Cuando Israel había hecho de nuevo lo malo, Dios los entregó a los madianitas, que se extendieron sobre la tierra como una nube de langostas, arrasando los campos y obligando al pueblo a refugiarse en cuevas y cavernas en los montes. Fue en aquella hora desesperada que Dios extendió su mano y llamó al más improbable de los libertadores: un agricultor atemorizado llamado Gedeón. Su historia es una de las lecciones más claras de toda la Escritura sobre cómo obra Dios: Él quita deliberadamente cada ventaja en que nos apoyamos, hasta que la única explicación posible para la victoria es Dios mismo. Cuando la batalla se gana con un puñado de hombres y sin espadas, nadie puede decir: «Mi mano me ha salvado».

blocks.en: Subject: Gideon — how God wins with few resources, so the glory is His alone.
blocks.es_reference: Tema: Gedeón — cómo Dios vence con pocos recursos, para que la gloria sea suya sola.

blocks.en: Proposition: God deliberately reduces our resources so that, when the victory comes, everyone knows the battle belonged to the Lord.
blocks.es_reference: Proposición: Dios reduce deliberadamente nuestros recursos para que, cuando venga la victoria, todos sepan que la batalla perteneció al Señor.

blocks.en: We will trace five movements in the story of Gideon.
blocks.es_reference: Trazaremos cinco movimientos en la historia de Gedeón.

blocks.en: I. The Timid Man
blocks.es_reference: I. El Hombre Tímido

blocks.en: When the Angel of the LORD found Gideon, he was threshing wheat by hiding it in a winepress, afraid the Midianites would steal it. And the greeting he received seems almost like a joke:
blocks.es_reference: Cuando el Ángel de Jehová encontró a Gedeón, este trillaba trigo escondiéndolo en un lagar, temiendo que los madianitas lo robaran. Y el saludo que recibió parece casi una broma:

blocks.en: The LORD is with you, you mighty man of valor! (Judges 6:12, NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: Jehová está contigo, varón esforzado y valiente. (Jueces 6:12, RVG)

blocks.en: A mighty man of valor — hiding in a winepress! But God does not call us according to what we are; He calls us according to what He will make of us. Gideon was anything but confident. He protested:
blocks.es_reference: ¡Un varón esforzado y valiente —escondido en un lagar! Pero Dios no nos llama según lo que somos; nos llama según lo que Él hará de nosotros. Gedeón era todo menos confiado. Protestó:

blocks.en: O my Lord, how can I save Israel? Indeed my clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father's house. (Judges 6:15, NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: Ah, Señor mío, ¿con qué tengo que salvar a Israel? He aquí que mi familia es pobre en Manasés, y yo el menor en la casa de mi padre. (Jueces 6:15, RVG)

blocks.en: That is exactly the kind of man God loves to use — one who knows he is nothing in himself. The Lord's answer did not flatter Gideon's strength; it promised God's presence: "Surely I will be with you, and you shall defeat the Midianites as one man." It is worth noting that the Gideons, who place Bibles in hotel rooms around the world, took their name from this timid, hesitant man — a fitting reminder that God uses the fearful who will simply trust Him. God meets the afraid right where they are.
blocks.es_reference: Ese es exactamente el tipo de hombre que a Dios le encanta usar —uno que sabe que no es nada en sí mismo—. La respuesta del Señor no halagó la fuerza de Gedeón; prometió la presencia de Dios: «Ciertamente yo estaré contigo, y herirás a los madianitas como a un solo hombre». Vale la pena notar que los Gedeones, que colocan Biblias en cuartos de hotel por todo el mundo, tomaron su nombre de este hombre tímido y vacilante —un recordatorio apropiado de que Dios usa a los temerosos que simplemente confían en Él—. Dios encuentra a los temerosos justo donde están.

blocks.en: II. Too Many to Boast
blocks.es_reference: II. Demasiados para Jactarse

blocks.en: When Gideon finally sounded the trumpet, thirty-two thousand men answered the call. By any human measure that was far too few to face the vast army of Midian, whose troops and camels lay in the valley as thick as locusts, beyond counting. But God said something astonishing: it was too many.
blocks.es_reference: Cuando Gedeón por fin tocó la trompeta, treinta y dos mil hombres respondieron al llamado. Según cualquier medida humana, eran muy pocos para enfrentar al vasto ejército de Madián, cuyas tropas y camellos yacían en el valle tan densos como langostas, sin número. Pero Dios dijo algo asombroso: eran demasiados.

blocks.en: The people who are with you are too many for Me to give the Midianites into their hands, lest Israel claim glory for itself against Me, saying, "My own hand has saved me." (Judges 7:2, NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: El pueblo que está contigo es mucho para que yo dé a los madianitas en su mano, no sea que se alabe Israel contra mí, diciendo: Mi mano me ha salvado. (Jueces 7:2, RVG)

blocks.en: Here is the heart of the whole matter. God was not worried that Gideon had too small an army; He was concerned that the army was too large — large enough that Israel might credit the victory to its own strength. The same truth rings out through the prophet Zechariah:
blocks.es_reference: Aquí está el corazón de todo el asunto. Dios no estaba preocupado de que Gedeón tuviera un ejército demasiado pequeño; le preocupaba que el ejército fuera demasiado grande —tan grande que Israel pudiera atribuir la victoria a su propia fuerza—. La misma verdad resuena por medio del profeta Zacarías:

blocks.en: Not by might nor by power, but by My Spirit, says the LORD of hosts. (Zechariah 4:6, NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: No con ejército, ni con fuerza, sino con mi Espíritu, ha dicho Jehová de los ejércitos. (Zacarías 4:6, RVG)

blocks.en: So God told Gideon to send home everyone who was afraid. Twenty-two thousand turned and left; only ten thousand remained. In a single command, two-thirds of the army was gone — and God was still not finished thinning the ranks.
blocks.es_reference: Así que Dios le dijo a Gedeón que enviara a casa a todo el que tuviera miedo. Veintidós mil dieron la vuelta y se fueron; solo quedaron diez mil. En un solo mandato, dos tercios del ejército desaparecieron —y Dios aún no había terminado de reducir las filas—.

blocks.en: III. The Water Test
blocks.es_reference: III. La Prueba del Agua

blocks.en: Ten thousand was still too many. God brought the men down to the water and gave Gideon a strange instruction: watch how they drink. Most of the men knelt down and put their faces to the water; but three hundred lifted the water to their mouths with their hands, lapping like a dog. Scripture does not explain why this particular manner of drinking mattered to God — only that by it, three hundred were set apart from the rest. Those three hundred — and only those — were the ones God would use.
blocks.es_reference: Diez mil todavía eran demasiados. Dios llevó a los hombres al agua y le dio a Gedeón una instrucción extraña: observa cómo beben. La mayoría de los hombres se arrodillaron y pusieron sus rostros en el agua; pero trescientos llevaron el agua a sus bocas con las manos, lamiendo como un perro. La Escritura no explica por qué esta manera particular de beber le importaba a Dios —solo que por ella, trescientos fueron apartados del resto. Esos trescientos —y solo esos— eran los que Dios usaría.

blocks.en: By the three hundred men who lapped I will save you, and deliver the Midianites into your hand. (Judges 7:7, NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: Con estos trescientos hombres que lamieron el agua os salvaré, y entregaré a los madianitas en tu mano. (Jueces 7:7, RVG)

blocks.en: From thirty-two thousand to three hundred — God had reduced the army to less than one in a hundred. To human eyes it was madness; to God it was perfect. He delights to take what the world would throw away and accomplish through it what no army could.
blocks.es_reference: De treinta y dos mil a trescientos —Dios había reducido el ejército a menos de uno por cada cien—. A ojos humanos era locura; para Dios era perfecto. Se deleita en tomar lo que el mundo desecharía y lograr por medio de ello lo que ningún ejército podría.

blocks.en: We see the same pattern long after Gideon. In the Nazi concentration camp of Ravensbrück, Corrie ten Boom and her sister Betsie were crowded into a flea-infested barracks. Betsie insisted they give thanks to God even for the fleas, taking the Scripture at its word: "In everything give thanks; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you" (1 Thessalonians 5:18). Corrie thought thanking God for fleas was absurd. Yet later they discovered that the guards refused to enter that barracks precisely because of the fleas — and so the two sisters were left free to read their Bible and pray and minister to the other women, week after week. What looked like a curse was the very thing God used for good. God's arithmetic is not ours; His three hundred are mightier than our thirty-two thousand.
blocks.es_reference: Vemos el mismo patrón mucho después de Gedeón. En el campo de concentración nazi de Ravensbrück, Corrie ten Boom y su hermana Betsie fueron amontonadas en un barracón infestado de pulgas. Betsie insistió en que dieran gracias a Dios aun por las pulgas, tomando la Escritura por su palabra: «Dad gracias en todo; porque esta es la voluntad de Dios para con vosotros en Cristo Jesús» (1 Tesalonicenses 5:18). A Corrie le parecía absurdo dar gracias por las pulgas. Pero más tarde descubrieron que los guardias se negaban a entrar en aquel barracón precisamente a causa de las pulgas —y así las dos hermanas quedaron libres para leer su Biblia, orar y ministrar a las otras mujeres, semana tras semana—. Lo que parecía una maldición era justamente lo que Dios usó para bien. La aritmética de Dios no es la nuestra; sus trescientos son más poderosos que nuestros treinta y dos mil.

blocks.en: IV. Faith Bolstered
blocks.es_reference: IV. La Fe Fortalecida

blocks.en: Even with the promise of God, Gideon was still afraid — and God was gentle with his fear. That night the Lord told him to creep down to the edge of the enemy camp and listen. There Gideon overheard one Midianite telling another his dream of a loaf of barley bread that came tumbling into the camp and flattened a tent. The other soldier answered:
blocks.es_reference: Aun con la promesa de Dios, Gedeón todavía tenía miedo —y Dios fue tierno con su temor—. Aquella noche el Señor le dijo que bajara sigilosamente al borde del campamento enemigo y escuchara. Allí Gedeón oyó a un madianita contándole a otro su sueño de un pan de cebada que venía rodando al campamento y derribaba una tienda. El otro soldado respondió:

blocks.en: This is nothing else but the sword of Gideon... for into his hand God has delivered Midian and the whole camp. (Judges 7:14, NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: Esto no es otra cosa sino la espada de Gedeón... Dios ha entregado en sus manos a los madianitas con todo el campamento. (Jueces 7:14, RVG)

blocks.en: The enemy themselves were already certain of their defeat. When Gideon heard it, he bowed and worshiped, and went back strengthened. God knows our weakness, and He often stoops to give the trembling believer just enough assurance to obey.
blocks.es_reference: Los mismos enemigos ya estaban seguros de su derrota. Cuando Gedeón lo oyó, se inclinó y adoró, y volvió fortalecido. Dios conoce nuestra debilidad, y muchas veces se inclina para dar al creyente tembloroso justo la seguridad suficiente para obedecer.

blocks.en: V. The Victory
blocks.es_reference: V. La Victoria

blocks.en: Then came the strangest battle plan ever given. Gideon divided his three hundred men into three companies and put into their hands — not swords and shields — but a trumpet in one hand and a clay pitcher with a burning torch hidden inside it in the other. At his signal, in the dead of night, they surrounded the camp, blew the trumpets, smashed the pitchers so the torches blazed out in the darkness, and shouted:
blocks.es_reference: Entonces vino el plan de batalla más extraño jamás dado. Gedeón dividió a sus trescientos hombres en tres compañías y puso en sus manos —no espadas y escudos— sino una trompeta en una mano y un cántaro de barro con una antorcha encendida escondida dentro en la otra. A su señal, en lo profundo de la noche, rodearon el campamento, tocaron las trompetas, quebraron los cántaros para que las antorchas resplandecieran en la oscuridad, y gritaron:

blocks.en: The sword of the LORD and of Gideon! (Judges 7:20, NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: ¡La espada de Jehová y de Gedeón! (Jueces 7:20, RVG)

blocks.en: Three hundred trumpets, three hundred shattered jars, three hundred sudden lights, and a single great shout — and the enemy was thrown into panic. In the confusion and darkness the Midianites turned their swords on one another and fled. Gideon's men did not even charge into the camp; every man simply stood in his place around it, holding torch and trumpet while God threw the enemy into confusion. In that first, decisive moment Israel had not struck a single blow with a sword — the initial rout came entirely through the Lord's intervention and the Midianites' own panic. Israel would still pursue and fight in the chapters that follow, but the battle had already been won before a single Israelite sword was drawn.
blocks.es_reference: Trescientas trompetas, trescientos cántaros rotos, trescientas luces repentinas, y un solo gran grito —y el enemigo fue arrojado al pánico—. En la confusión y la oscuridad los madianitas volvieron sus espadas unos contra otros y huyeron. Los hombres de Gedeón ni siquiera cargaron contra el campamento; cada uno simplemente se mantuvo en su lugar alrededor de él, sosteniendo su antorcha y su trompeta mientras Dios sembraba la confusión en el enemigo. En ese primer momento decisivo, Israel no había dado un solo golpe con la espada —la desbandada inicial vino enteramente de la intervención del Señor y del pánico de los propios madianitas—. Israel todavía perseguiría y pelearía en los capítulos que siguen, pero la batalla ya estaba ganada antes de que un solo israelita desenvainara su espada.

blocks.en: The Battle Belongs to the Lord
blocks.es_reference: La Batalla es del Señor

blocks.en: This is the lesson God wants us to learn: He thins our resources so that the victory can only be His. Surrendered obedience, not human strategy, wins the day.
blocks.es_reference: Esta es la lección que Dios quiere que aprendamos: Él reduce nuestros recursos para que la victoria solo pueda ser suya. La obediencia rendida, no la estrategia humana, gana el día.

blocks.en: I learned this myself in a season when our family had almost nothing. We had three small boys and about seven hundred dollars to our name when my wife wrecked our old station wagon. Too stubborn to accept help, I tried to scheme my own way out. But some men from the Gideons in Louisiana insisted on helping, and one of them said to me, "If the Lord is leading me to help you, you don't have any right to turn it down." In the end God provided a far better car at half the mileage; a mechanic paid me five hundred dollars for the wreck; and a man in the church carried the rest at three percent interest. I said I was waiting on the Lord, but the truth is I was still scheming in my own mind the whole time. This battle belonged to the Lord, and none of my scheming was necessary.
blocks.es_reference: Yo mismo aprendí esto en una temporada en que nuestra familia casi no tenía nada. Teníamos tres niños pequeños y unos setecientos dólares a nuestro nombre cuando mi esposa chocó nuestra vieja camioneta. Demasiado terco para aceptar ayuda, traté de tramar mi propia salida. Pero unos hombres de los Gedeones en Luisiana insistieron en ayudar, y uno de ellos me dijo: «Si el Señor me está guiando a ayudarte, no tienes ningún derecho a rechazarlo». Al final Dios proveyó un auto mucho mejor con la mitad del kilometraje; un mecánico me pagó quinientos dólares por el vehículo chocado; y un hombre de la iglesia llevó el resto al tres por ciento de interés. Yo decía que esperaba en el Señor, pero la verdad es que seguía tramando en mi propia mente todo el tiempo. Esta batalla pertenecía al Señor, y nada de mis tramas era necesario.

blocks.en: Whatever the Midianites are in your life — whatever enemy looks too large and whatever resources look too small — remember Gideon's three hundred. God is not looking for the strong; He is looking for the willing, that He may show Himself strong on their behalf. The same God who emptied Gideon's hands of every weapon but a trumpet and a torch can be trusted with your empty hands as well. So often we say we are waiting on the Lord while we are still scheming in our hearts for a way out, as I once did with that wrecked car in Louisiana; but His victory does not depend on our cleverness. Lay down the scheming, take up simple obedience, and follow the One who has already won. When you have few resources, the battle still belongs to the Lord.
blocks.es_reference: Cualquiera que sean los madianitas en tu vida —cualquier enemigo que parezca demasiado grande y cualesquiera recursos que parezcan demasiado pocos— recuerda los trescientos de Gedeón. Dios no busca a los fuertes; busca a los dispuestos, para mostrarse fuerte a favor de ellos. El mismo Dios que vació las manos de Gedeón de toda arma salvo una trompeta y una antorcha también es digno de confianza con tus manos vacías. Muchas veces decimos que esperamos en el Señor mientras seguimos tramando en el corazón una salida, como yo lo hice con aquel auto chocado en Luisiana; pero su victoria no depende de nuestra astucia. Deja el tramar, toma la sencilla obediencia, y sigue a Aquel que ya ganó. Cuando tienes pocos recursos, la batalla todavía pertenece al Señor.

mc.stem: To whom did God hand Israel over in the days of Gideon?
mc.why: Because Israel had done evil, God gave them into the hand of the Midianites, who oppressed the land.

mc.stem: The Midianite oppressors are compared to what?
options: A swarm of locusts covering the land
mc.why: The Midianites swept over the land like locusts, stripping the fields and driving Israel into hiding.

mc.stem: When the Angel of the LORD found Gideon, what was he doing?
options: Threshing wheat in a winepress, hiding it from the Midianites
mc.why: Gideon was threshing wheat in a winepress out of fear that the Midianites would steal it.

mc.stem: How did the Angel of the LORD greet Gideon?
options: "The LORD is with you, you mighty man of valor!"
mc.why: The greeting "mighty man of valor" was spoken to a man hiding in a winepress — God calls us according to what He will make of us.

mc.stem: How did Gideon describe himself when God called him?
options: The strongest man in his tribe
The least in his father's house, from the weakest clan in Manasseh
mc.why: Gideon saw himself as the least and weakest — exactly the kind of person God delights to use.

mc.stem: What did God promise Gideon in answer to his fear?
options: "Surely I will be with you, and you shall defeat the Midianites as one man"
That a great army would gather from every tribe
That he would never face any danger
That another man would fight in his place
mc.why: God's answer was not to flatter Gideon's strength but to promise His own presence.

mc.stem: How many men first answered Gideon's call to fight?
mc.why: Thirty-two thousand answered — far too few by human measure, yet God called them too many.

mc.stem: Why did God say Gideon's army was too many?
options: There was not enough food for them
So Israel could not boast, "My own hand has saved me"
The Midianites were too few to fight
mc.why: God was concerned the army was large enough that Israel might claim the glory for itself.

mc.stem: Which verse captures the principle behind Gideon's victory?
options: "The battle is long but the reward is sure"
"Not by might nor by power, but by My Spirit, says the LORD of hosts"
mc.why: Zechariah 4:6 states the heart of the story: God's work is done by His Spirit, not human might.

mc.stem: In the first reduction, whom did God send home, and how many remained?
mc.why: God sent home all who were afraid; 22,000 left and 10,000 remained — and He was not finished.

mc.stem: At the water, which men did God choose to keep?
options: The 300 who lapped the water with their hands, like a dog
Those who knelt down to drink
Those who refused to drink at all
mc.why: The 300 who lapped from their hands, staying alert, were the ones God would use.

mc.stem: How many men did God finally use to defeat Midian?
mc.why: From 32,000 to 300 — less than one in a hundred, so the victory could only be God's.

mc.stem: Why did God deliberately reduce Gideon's army?
options: To make the battle last longer
Because most of the men had sinned
So the victory could only be credited to God, not to man
To save supplies for the journey
mc.why: God strips away our advantages so that the only explanation for victory is God Himself.

mc.stem: What did Gideon overhear that strengthened his faith?
options: An enemy soldier's dream of a barley loaf, interpreted as "the sword of Gideon"
mc.why: The enemy themselves were already certain of defeat; hearing it, Gideon was strengthened.

mc.stem: What did Gideon do after overhearing the enemy's dream?
options: He bowed and worshiped, then returned strengthened
mc.why: Gideon worshiped God in response to the assurance, then went back ready to obey.

mc.stem: What did Gideon's 300 carry into battle?
options: Trumpets and torches hidden inside clay pitchers — no swords in hand
mc.why: Each man held a trumpet and a torch hidden in a clay pitcher — not a weapon of war.

mc.stem: What was the battle cry of Gideon's men?
options: "The sword of the LORD and of Gideon!"
mc.why: They blew the trumpets, broke the pitchers, and cried, "The sword of the LORD and of Gideon!"

mc.stem: What happened to the Midianite army?
options: They panicked, turned their swords on one another, and fled
mc.why: In the darkness and confusion the Midianites destroyed one another in that first, decisive rout; Israel struck no blow with a sword in that opening moment, though pursuit and real combat followed in the chapters after.

mc.stem: What is the lesson of Corrie ten Boom's fleas at Ravensbrück?
options: Suffering is always punishment for sin
Give thanks in everything — the fleas God used kept the guards out, leaving the sisters free to read the Bible and pray
God never allows His people to suffer
mc.why: What looked like a curse was the very thing God used for good (1 Thessalonians 5:18).

mc.stem: What is the central lesson of Gideon's story?
options: God reduces our resources so the victory is clearly His — the battle belongs to the Lord
Only the strong are useful to God
mc.why: God thins our resources so the victory can only be His; surrendered obedience wins the day.

sa.prompt: Why did God tell Gideon that his 32,000 men were too many?
sa.model: God said the army was too many so that Israel could not boast, "My own hand has saved me." With a large army the people would credit the victory to their own strength rather than to God. God was not worried that Gideon had too few men; He was concerned the army was large enough to rob Him of the glory. So He reduced it until only He could be praised.

sa.prompt: Describe the water test and what it accomplished.
sa.model: At the water God watched how the men drank. Most knelt and put their faces to the water, but three hundred lifted it with their hands and lapped like a dog while staying alert. God kept only those three hundred and sent the rest home. The test reduced the army from ten thousand to three hundred, so the victory would clearly belong to God and not to a large force.

sa.prompt: What does Zechariah 4:6 teach about how God's work is accomplished?
sa.model: Zechariah 4:6 says, "Not by might nor by power, but by My Spirit, says the LORD of hosts." It teaches that God's work is accomplished by His Spirit, not by human might or power. Gideon's story is this verse lived out: the victory came not through a strong army but through God working with a tiny, surrendered band. We are to depend on God's Spirit rather than on our own strength.

sa.prompt: How did God strengthen Gideon's faith just before the battle?
sa.model: Though still afraid, Gideon was told to creep down to the enemy camp and listen. There he overheard a Midianite tell a dream of a barley loaf tumbling into the camp, which his comrade interpreted as the sword of Gideon, to whom God had given the victory. The enemy themselves were certain of defeat. When Gideon heard it, he bowed and worshiped and went back strengthened to obey. God is gentle with our fear and gives just enough assurance to act.

sa.prompt: Describe the battle, and explain why the victory was clearly God's.
sa.model: Gideon divided his three hundred into three companies, each man holding a trumpet and a torch hidden in a clay pitcher instead of a sword. At night they surrounded the camp, blew the trumpets, broke the pitchers so the torches blazed, and cried, "The sword of the LORD and of Gideon!" The Midianites panicked, turned their swords on one another, and fled. Israel struck no blow with a sword, so the victory was plainly the Lord's.

sa.prompt: What is the lesson of Corrie ten Boom's fleas, and how does it relate to Gideon?
sa.model: In Ravensbrück, Betsie insisted they thank God even for the fleas in their barracks, obeying the command to give thanks in everything. Later they learned the guards would not enter because of the fleas, leaving the sisters free to read the Bible and pray. What seemed a curse was God's provision for good. Like Gideon's three hundred, it shows that God's arithmetic is not ours; He uses what we would reject to accomplish His purposes.

sa.prompt: What does the Louisiana car testimony illustrate about trusting God?
sa.model: With three small boys and almost no money, the family lost their car, and the preacher was too stubborn to accept help while quietly scheming his own way out. Yet some Gideons insisted on helping, God provided a far better car, a mechanic paid for the wreck, and a church member carried the rest. He had said he was waiting on the Lord while still scheming, but in the end none of his scheming was necessary. The battle belonged to the Lord, just as it had for Gideon.

sa.prompt: What kind of person does God look for, according to Gideon's story, and why?
sa.model: God does not look for the strong or self-confident but for the willing — those who know they are nothing in themselves. Gideon was timid, weak, and afraid, the least in his father's house, yet God used him. The Lord chooses such people so that the glory clearly belongs to Him and not to human strength. He is looking for the available, that He may show Himself strong on their behalf.

sa.prompt: State the main proposition of this lesson in your own words.
sa.model: The proposition is that God deliberately reduces our resources so that, when the victory comes, everyone knows the battle belonged to the Lord. He thins what we lean on until only He can be credited. Gideon's army shrank from thirty-two thousand to three hundred for exactly this reason. God wins with few so the glory is His alone.

sa.prompt: How does Gideon's story apply when you face a large problem with few resources?
sa.model: When the enemy looks too large and our resources look too small, Gideon's story tells us to trust God and obey Him rather than scheme our own way out. Few resources are no obstacle to God; in fact He often prefers them, so the victory is plainly His. We surrender our weakness to Him and follow His instructions, even strange ones. When we have little, the battle still belongs to the Lord.
